recommendation: Prioritise by income first; the onboarding model re-ranks within income bands
evidence: A single income threshold (about Rs 122,249/yr, re-learned per fold) is the reference. At a 25% contact budget the headline model reaches 36.2% of at-risk households (98.5% of the 36.7% ceiling) against 35.0% for the income rule (95.4% of ceiling): +1.1 pp, 95% CI 1.0 to 1.3.
caveat: The model refines an income ranking; it does not discover a hidden at-risk segment.

recommendation: Judge targeting against the ceiling and the income rule, not against random contact
evidence: With 68.1% of households at risk, no strategy can reach more than 36.7% of them with a 25% budget. Precision at 25%: headline model 98.5%, income rule 95.4% (difference +3.1 pp, CI 2.7 to 3.6); random 67.8%.
caveat: Lift over random looks impressive only because the at-risk class is the majority.

recommendation: Do not size a budgeting product from peer benchmarks
evidence: Whether at-risk households could close their gap by spending like on-track peers at the same income depends on how the benchmark is built: 92.8% could by matching peers' rupee spending, 22.3% by matching their budget shares. The rupee version is close to a tautology (at-risk means a larger budget at the same income). Median gap Rs 37,114/yr.
caveat: The pre-audit claim that the shortfall is structural for 71.5% of at-risk households is withdrawn; IHDS cannot separate structural from behavioural shortfall.

recommendation: Miscellaneous is not 'the' lever: budget composition differs most in healthcare and education
evidence: Signed mean share excess vs same-income on-track peers (95% PSU-bootstrap CI): Healthcare +4.4 pp (+3.8 to +4.9); Education +2.8 pp (+2.7 to +3.0); Miscellaneous +2.1 pp (+1.7 to +2.5); Transport +1.8 pp (+1.5 to +2.1); Groceries -9.0 pp. Miscellaneous ranks 3 of 8 categories with a significant positive share excess.
caveat: Excess vs peers is a hypothesis about slack, not evidence that spending is optional. Rupee totals (e.g. Miscellaneous Rs 51 crore/yr) are sample totals over surveyed households, not population figures.

recommendation: Report relative priority only - never an absolute prevalence figure
evidence: 22.0% of households report spending more than twice their income and are 32.3% of the at-risk group. Moving the benchmark to 10% or 30% moves the at-risk share to 61.7% or 74.7%.
caveat: Any claim that 'X% of Indian households save inadequately' is unsupported by this work.
